summary:
Malaysia criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity at both federal and state level. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature", covering oral and anal sex, for any person regardless of gender, consent or whether the act is private; the maximum penalty is 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping, and Human Rights Watch records the whipping as mandatory. The offence reaches foreign nationals and tourists, and sodomy was first criminalised in 1871. Section 377D adds "gross indecency", an undefined offence carrying up to two years that remains a discretionary prosecutorial tool.

Every state and the federal territories maintain Sharia enactments criminalising same-sex activity and gender nonconformity, including provisions against "a man posing as a woman". These offences apply only to Muslims, so a Muslim trans visitor carries exposure that a non-Muslim visitor does not; the penalties reach three years' imprisonment, a RM5,000 fine and six strokes of the cane. The enactments include the Selangor and Kelantan codes and the Sharia Criminal Code (I) Enactment 2019, which covers sodomy and sexual intercourse against the order of nature. Since the 1980s all 13 states have passed such enactments; all 13 bar Muslim men from dressing as women, three also bar women posing as men, and none supplies a legal definition of transgender dress. Enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments.

Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted, but that pattern is prosecutorial discretion rather than legal protection, and it has been withdrawn under political pressure. Raids on queer venues are documented and current: on 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur and arrested 208 men under section 377B, the largest such raid since 2022, with media pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details leaked; 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground under 377B, yet releases were delayed, with over 130 men still held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Police raided a second sauna in Penang days later. Earlier actions include a Kuala Lumpur gay bar raided by police and religious enforcement in August 2018, a Halloween party with LGBTQ participants raided in 2022, and 11 shopping malls raided in May 2023 over pride-themed watches.

Trans people face documented state-sanctioned targeting. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced he had given the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists condemned and demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her over "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and obtained UNHCR protection. Violence accompanies this: a transgender woman was killed in Klang in 2019, the third such killing of a trans woman in Malaysia in fewer than two months, in a record that also documents police mistreatment and impunity. Sixteen trans women were mass-arrested at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Identity documents are a live exposure point. The Registration Department routinely rejects gender-marker changes. In August 2016 the Kuala Lumpur High Court ordered the National Registration Department to update a trans man's identity card with his gender identity and chosen name, reasoning that Article 5(1) of the Federal Constitution guarantees a right to live with dignity as a male, but that judgment was overturned on appeal in 2017. The only successful documented gender-marker change is historical: in 1975 the National Registration Department recognised a trans woman as female and the Johor Deputy Mufti allowed her to marry under sharia law. A 1982 National Fatwa Committee edict holds that sex is determined at birth and remains so after sex reassignment surgery; it was never gazetted and is not legally binding, but it ended domestic sex-reassignment surgery and shapes administrative practice.

The sources contain no explicit visa or entry rule for transgender visitors. The only stated entry policy is a 2001 remark by then-Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad that Malaysia would deport any visiting foreign cabinet minister or diplomat who is gay and warning gay foreign ministers not to bring their partners.

Detention carries prescribed custodial and "rehabilitation" facilities. Sharia courts may commit women convicted of musahaqah to an approved home for up to six months under Federal Territories s.56, Kedah s.52, Selangor s.54 and Sarawak s.53, and may order cross-dressing or other offenders into counselling or rehabilitation in a religious institution for up to six months under Kelantan s.19-20 and Pahang s.66, extended to one year by Terengganu's 2022 amendment. Prison terms for Sharia offences run from four months to three years and are served in male wards where sexual violence is documented. Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021.

Access to care is restricted. Conversion therapy is practised regularly and openly promoted by politicians and religious leaders, the 1982 fatwa bars Muslims from sex reassignment surgery unless intersex, transgender people face discriminatory denial of health care and employment, and the National Blood Centre of Malaysia prohibits homosexuals and bisexuals from donating blood.

There are no Malaysian laws protecting the LGBTQ community against discrimination and hate crimes, and no route to recognition for same-sex couples. The High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional. Hate speech rules do cover orientation through the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Content Code 2022, s.6.1(ii), enforced via s.211 of the Communications and Multimedia Act, while in 1994 the government banned anyone homosexual, bisexual or transsexual from state-controlled media and LGBT events and media content continue to be censored.
tangentialFactors:
Reform prospects are foreclosed by Islamist opposition pressure, which Human Rights Watch reported in August 2023 as deepening fear among LGBT people and closing off legislative change.

Federalism litigation has produced narrow wins without decriminalising anything: the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024, both on federalism grounds, leaving the Penal Code offences fully intact.

On 2 December 2025 the Home Minister floated revisiting the section 377 provisions, days before the Penang sauna raid. The sources do not resolve whether any amendment followed.

Kelantan approved amendments to its entertainment law in November 2024 banning activities that promote LGBTQ behaviour, adding a venue-level restriction to the existing offence provisions.

The Human Dignity Trust places Malaysia among jurisdictions that criminalise same-sex conduct and lists active litigation in the country alongside cases from Mauritius and Namibia.

Censorship of LGBT events and media content is documented alongside the 1994 statutory-adjacent ban on LGBT people in state-controlled media, and in 2019 no political party pursues LGBTQ rights according to the sources; Mahathir told the Cambridge Union in June 2019 that Malaysia cannot accept same-sex marriage, calling it "a regressive way of thinking".
localsOnly:
All 13 states have passed Sharia enactments institutionalising discrimination against trans people since the 1980s, enforced by state Islamic religious departments with no legal definition of transgender dressing. Three of the 13 also bar "women posing as men".

Enforcement history includes the 2011 strip-search and sexual assault of a trans woman named Victoria by religious officials, repeated arrests of one woman exceeding 20 times, and the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014 that triggered the Negeri Sembilan constitutional challenge, with the Court of Appeal decision then expected on 7 November 2014.

Transgender people face discriminatory denial of health care and employment alongside arbitrary arrest, physical and sexual assault, and imprisonment; prison terms of four months to three years are served in male wards where sexual violence is documented.

Conversion therapy is practised regularly and promoted openly by politicians and religious leaders. The 1982 fatwa bars Muslims from sex reassignment surgery unless intersex and rules marriages involving transgender people invalid, though it was never gazetted and is not legally binding.

The Registration Department routinely rejects gender-marker changes, and the 2016 Kuala Lumpur High Court order requiring an identity-card update was overturned on appeal in 2017.

There is no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection for LGBTQ residents. The National Blood Centre of Malaysia prohibits homosexuals and bisexuals from donating blood in a policy that appears gender neutral, and anyone homosexual, bisexual or transsexual has been barred from state-controlled media since 1994.

Same-sex couples have no route to recognition. The single exception in the record is the 1975 sharia marriage of a transgender woman in Johor Bahru. Adoption is orientation-neutral: under the Adoption Act 1952 and the Registration of Adoption Act 1952 there is no restriction on a single person adopting regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid for those held after the November 2025 sauna raid. Seventeen civil servants identified in the leaked detainee details were suspended.
outOfScopeNotes:
No background or general homicide rate is sourced for Malaysia, so the 2019 killings of trans women cannot be placed against a population-level comparison; the sources document the incidents, police mistreatment and impunity without a denominator.

No explicit visa or entry rule specific to transgender visitors appears in the sources. The 2001 statement about deporting gay foreign ministers is the only entry policy recorded, and its current status is not sourced.

The 1982 fatwa was never gazetted, so its formal legal weight remains unresolved even though it ended domestic sex-reassignment surgery and is applied by administrators.

The joint United Nations Development Programme and Asia Pacific Transgender Network publication on Malaysia is listed without its findings, so no claim is drawn from it.

No youth-specific health-care or medication-carrying finding appears in the sources.
